comment_text.value:
Most of my time building feels like a dance across (i) Claude/Codex TUIs (ii) Github PRs and (iii) Jira/Linear/etc issues. The greater the parallelization, the more intricate the dance feels. At some point, parallel work on N issues leads to 3*N windows. OS window management starts to feel cumbersome and ultimately constraining. You can go a bit further with things like using different desktops, one per project, and at least only seeing the windows of one project at a time.

I’ve looked into agent orchestration tools like Herdr, Emdash, Conductor, Superset but felt features most useful to me were spread across them. Herdr is built more around agents and panes and less around issues. The rest may come closer with linking PRs and issues, but they’re desktop apps. Claude Code’s agent view is good for hopping between sessions, but it doesn’t currently address the window overload problem.

My preference for the Claude/Codex TUIs over the desktop versions nudged me to explore what blend of the two I can get away with. This led to a Rust shell where the issue and PR sit beside a Claude/Codex session. It’s a TUI with its prefix key etc. that also supports less traditionally-TUI things like drag-to-reorder for projects/issues. It’s a Claude/Codex++ designed around multiple sessions and minimizing chasing windows or alt-tabbing. Ultimately, it remains an extension over my Claude/Codex TUI experience and helps with the multitasking dance across different live threads. Curious if this approach or even problem statement resonates with others.

Happy to answer questions and feedback is very welcome!

story_title.value: Show HN: Built Taskman, a Rust TUI for Parallel Claude/Codex Work on Issues+PRs

comment_text.value:
I don’t know about bigger projects but for my smallish solo project I have a single STATUS.md. Agents are instructed to read it first and update it at every session/commit. It’s the main handoff document and I had no problem switching between Claude Code and Codex agents.

There is a sprint based roadmap doc. We do sprint planning and each sprint has multiple sessions with session numbers. There is a backlog document to keep track of all the bugs and feature ideas. There are many ADR documents (Architectural Decision Records) which I admit can become stale in time, but Claude is quick to notice because it actually reads these. They are the main contract between us. For a new feature an ADR is written before writing any code or an old one is amended.

I assumed this was a common workflow because I just prompted Claude to setup the project using its own best practices for a lightweight document-driven development.

I believe asking the model itself is better than using a random repo. These things have access to and trained on an enormous number of projects. They know what they need.

story_title.value: Agents don't need memory, they need documentation

comment_text.value:
We used Claude Code agents running Opus 5 with each of the 12 memory systems. Each agent got the same work across multiple sessions and 150 questions.

Each memory tool runs through weeks of simulated work. Each agent chooses what to store and remember, guided by each tool’s own documentation.

Cognee and Karpathy’s Wiki tied for the highest accuracy score at 97.1 out of 100.

Using Cognee is significantly cheaper, at about half the wiki’s token cost at $256 per 1,000 questions vs. $503.

Every memory system has tradeoffs though, Cognee was the slowest system we tested, taking over five times as long per question as the wiki.

Across the tests, the biggest reason for failure was agents declining to answer questions they should have been able to answer. That accounted for 61% of failures.

We also tested whether each system leaked information it had been told to forget. 9/12 systems never repeated the facts they’d been told to forget, while three leaked data that should have been forgotten.

comment_text.value:
The problem is that, as seen in the case of the Houthi rebels developing missile software using Claude Code, AI has lowered the very threshold at which human cruelty or selfishness can be put into practice. Anthropic’s safeguards were applied on a per-request basis, but splitting the work into multiple sessions prevented me from seeing the bigger picture. After all, human instinct does not transform into technology, so the only remaining way is to pile up the friction that takes that instinct to turn into action all over again.

However, the international agreement proposed by Dario Amodei is ultimately nothing more than a promise made by people. There is also a precedent in which the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty could have simply withdrawn if it had been cornered like North Korea. Isn’t the AI speed-control agreement also vulnerable to being broken in the same way if one side finds itself politically cornered. In particular, unlike nuclear weapons, AI has the characteristic of recursively improving itself, allowing its capabilities to accelerate itself, so the moment one side breaks away, the gap can widen in an instant, making the incentive for deviation even greater.

With grok bot, I've just been giving it a time to stop working; otherwise, it's likely to burn through my entire week's usage in an afternoon.

If I want to run multiple sessions in parallel in claude code and codex, I use multiple worktrees, and I select tasks for each tree that are unlikely to have merge conflicts.

story_title.value: Ask HN: What are your biggest problems and fixes with multisession engineering?
